implementation_notes: Structured concurrency replaces the router object: inside coroutineScope the runtime recipient list is mapped to async Deferreds and awaitAll resumes when every copy has been delivered, or fails immediately - including cancellation of the siblings - as soon as one delivery throws. Dispatchers.IO is where blocking clients belong, and supervisorScope (or a per-recipient runCatching) is what turns the fan-out into continue-on-error. A hand-written router is still justified when recipient resolution and delivery policy must be reused by several services, but the concurrency mechanics themselves never are.
pitfalls: awaitAll fails as soon as one deferred fails and cancels its siblings, so a single broken recipient aborts the remaining deliveries; supervisorScope or runCatching is required for continue-on-error.
async inherits the caller's dispatcher - a blocking send without Dispatchers.IO occupies a CPU-bound thread and can stall unrelated coroutines.
Iterating a mutable recipient collection while the fan-out is running races with it; take a snapshot (toList()) before mapping to async.
